case_title: Munnawar and Ors. v. State of U.P. Etc.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 read with s.149 (conviction); s.307 (originally charged and convicted at trial)
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony; dying declarations (by police officer and executive magistrate); medical evidence (treating doctor and post-mortem); recovery of pistols; ballistic expert (defence witness)
aggravating_circumstances: Close-range firing (tattooing present); multiple wounds, several grievous and fatal, on sensitive parts of the body
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.307, sentenced to 4 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs.5,000 each; acquitted under s.302
high_court_outcome: Accused's appeal dismissed; State appeal allowed; convicted under s.302/149 IPC and sentenced to life imprisonment
neutral_facts: The victim and two companions were travelling to a court hearing by bus, got off at about 11:15 a.m. at a bus stand, and walked towards the courts. Near the office of a bus union, several men armed with country-made pistols fired at the victim, who was seriously injured. The two companions ran to a nearby bus stand and the assailants fled. One companion took the victim to a hospital, where a doctor examined him at 11:35 a.m. and found him irritable but mentally conscious. A first information report was lodged about noon at a police station about two furlongs from the scene. A police sub-inspector recorded a statement from the victim at the hospital. The next day, an executive magistrate recorded a second dying declaration in the hospital in the presence of a doctor, who certified that the victim was fully conscious and lucid. The declaration named the assailants and the weapons used and described the site of the injuries. The victim died five days after the incident from septicemia following the gunshot injury. A post-mortem examination was conducted. Two country-made pistols were recovered at the instance of two of the accused. Medical evidence recorded seven wounds on the chest, neck, face, arm and back, with tattooing indicating close-range firing. Some wounds were grievous and fatal to life, and the victim had been given three units of blood on admission. A defence ballistic expert testified that a retained bullet could cause septicemia.
physical_harm: Death of the victim five days after the incident from septicemia following gunshot injuries; seven lacerated gunshot wounds (chest, neck, face, left hand, left forearm, right and left scapular regions), some grievous and fatal to life
number_of_offences: 2 charged (IPC s.302 and s.307; s.149 applied by High Court); 1 finally upheld (s.302/149)
key_evidence_accepted: Second dying declaration recorded by the Executive Magistrate and endorsed by the attending doctor; presence of the two eyewitnesses; prompt FIR; medical evidence of the treating doctor on injuries and cause of death
witness_credibility: Eyewitnesses found present at the scene; Magistrate and doctor found credible with no reason to disbelieve them; police officer's first dying declaration not relied on as the sole basis; treating doctor's evidence found independent and supportive
post_offence_conduct: Assailants fled the scene; one accused (Yaqoob) absconded during the investigation
trial_duration: offence: 20 May 2000; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 08 August 2007; Supreme Court: 5 May 2010
legal_representation: Accused: Sushil Kumar, Manoj Prasad, Aditya Kumar. State: T.N. Singh, Rajiv Dubey, Kamlendra Mishra
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; charge-sheet filed; trial completed; accused convicted at trial and in High Court
procedural_irregularity: Delay in delivery of special report to Magistrate (held not of consequence); first statement recorded by police officer in case diary not recorded in manner prescribed by Police Regulations for dying declarations (held not decisive given second declaration)
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted s.307, acquitted s.302. High Court: accused's appeal dismissed; State appeal allowed, convicted s.302/149 and life imprisonment. Supreme Court: appeals dismissed, conviction upheld
prosecution_argument: Promptness of FIR belies claim that eyewitnesses were brought to scene later; second dying declaration reliable though first was not; medical evidence shows injuries were the proximate cause of death despite time lag
defence_argument: First dying declaration lacked victim's signature and doctor's fitness endorsement; second declaration not properly endorsed and unreliable under Balak Ram; victim admitted by police officer, so eyewitnesses were not present; death from negligent treatment, so at most s.307 applies
legal_principle_applied: A dying declaration recorded by a Magistrate and endorsed by a doctor should not be discarded save for very good reasons; reliability depends on the facts of each case, with no hard and fast rule
precedent_relied_upon: Balak Ram v. State of U.P. (1975) 3 SCC 219; K. Ramachandra Reddy & Anr. v. Public Prosecutor (1976) 3 SCC 618
